items.title: Level 4: How the five Success Profiles elements fit together
items.body: Success Profiles is the Civil Service framework for describing what a job needs and how candidates are assessed. It has five elements. Behaviours are the actions and activities that show whether someone can do the job well, such as Working Together. Strengths are the things a person does regularly, does well and enjoys. Ability is the mental capacity or aptitude to carry out tasks, and it is often measured with tests, for instance numerical or verbal reasoning. Technical means the professional skills or qualifications a role requires, which matters for jobs such as accountancy but rarely for entry-level administration. Experience means the knowledge and understanding gained from working in a particular area. A department does not have to assess all five for each job. It chooses the elements that best fit the role and says which ones in the advert. For an Administrative Officer role, it is common to see an application sift on behaviours or experience, an online test of ability, and then an interview on behaviours and sometimes strengths. This is why you should read the advert for the assessment plan rather than assume. The elements can overlap in practice. A story about handling a busy phone line can show experience of customer work and the behaviour Managing a Quality Service at the same time. Knowing the difference helps you decide what the panel is looking for in each question. If it is a behaviour, give evidence of what you did. If it is a strength, answer naturally and briefly. If it is experience, describe what you have done and what you know.

questions.prompt: Which Success Profiles element describes the aptitude to carry out tasks and is often measured by tests?

options.text: Ability
Technical
Strengths
Experience

questions.hint: Ability is commonly measured by tests such as numerical reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which element is defined as things a person does regularly, does well and enjoys?

options.text: Technical
Experience
Strengths
Behaviours

questions.hint: This is the definition of strengths.

questions.prompt: Why is the Technical element rarely the main focus for entry-level administration roles?

options.text: Technical skills are only judged at senior grades by rule
Entry-level staff are not permitted to use technical systems
Technical skills are assessed only once a person has been appointed
Such roles seldom need specialist professional qualifications

questions.hint: Technical covers professional skills and qualifications, which entry roles seldom need.

questions.prompt: Where should you look to find which elements will be assessed for a particular job?

options.text: The general GOV.UK page covering all Civil Service jobs
The assessment plan in the job advert
The invitation email sent a week after the closing date
The department's annual report for the previous year

questions.hint: The advert states what will be assessed.

questions.prompt: A department assesses an AO role with an online test followed by an interview. Which element does the test most likely measure?

options.text: Experience
Strengths
Ability
Behaviours

questions.hint: Online reasoning tests measure ability.

questions.prompt: Why can one story count as both experience and a behaviour?

options.text: The same event can show what you know and how you acted
Experience and behaviours are two names for one thing
Panels score every story twice as a matter of rule
Behaviours can only be shown through paid experience

questions.hint: One story can show knowledge and a behaviour together.

questions.prompt: If a panel asks about a strength, how should you answer?

options.text: Naturally and briefly, showing what you enjoy
With a detailed STAR account of one past event
With a list of your qualifications and training
With a statement copied from your application form

questions.hint: Strengths answers should be natural and short.

questions.prompt: If a panel asks about your experience, what should you describe?

options.text: What you would do if you were in charge
What other people on your team say about you
What you have done and what you know about the area
What you hope to learn once you are in the job

questions.hint: Experience questions explore what you have done and know.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the five elements is correct?

options.text: Candidates choose which elements are used to assess them
Only behaviours can ever be assessed at an interview
Every job must assess all five elements to the same degree
A department chooses the elements that best fit the role

questions.hint: Departments select the elements for each role.

questions.prompt: What does a behaviour show, according to Success Profiles?

options.text: Whether someone enjoys the work done by the department
Whether someone holds the right qualifications for the job
Whether someone can do the job well, through their actions
Whether someone has worked in government before

questions.hint: Behaviours are actions that show effectiveness.

items.title: Level 4: Reading what a behaviour question really asks
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Strong candidates read a question carefully before answering. Consider 'Tell us about a time you had to explain something complicated to someone who was struggling to understand.' There are several parts. The verb is 'explain', which points to Communicating and Influencing. The object is 'something complicated', so choose an example where the content was difficult. The person is 'struggling to understand', so the story needs to show you noticing and responding to that. Many candidates answer only part of the question. They explain a process but never say how they noticed the person was confused. Practise underlining the key phrases in practice questions and make sure your story covers each one. Some questions contain a second hidden request. 'Describe a time you had to work with someone you found difficult' is also asking how you stayed professional. 'Tell us about a time you had to change your plans' is asking how you coped with change and kept things on track. Questions can also combine behaviours. 'Tell us about a time you had to deliver a task quickly without losing quality' tests both Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service. If you are not sure what a question wants, it is fine to ask. You might say, 'Do you mean an example from work, or can it be from elsewhere?' Panels usually answer that any real example is welcome. Never reply with a general statement such as 'I always work well in a team.' The panel needs a specific moment.

questions.prompt: In the question 'Tell us about a time you had to explain something complicated to someone', which behaviour does the verb 'explain' point to?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Communicating and Influencing
Making Effective Decisions
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: Explaining links to Communicating and Influencing.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase 'struggling to understand' require your story to include?

options.text: The name and job title of the person you helped
How you noticed the difficulty and responded to it
The date and place of the conversation
A list of everything that you explained to them

questions.hint: The story should show you noticing and adapting.

questions.prompt: Which mistake do many candidates make with a question like this?

options.text: They mention the other person by name
They give too much detail about the result
They use too many examples from outside work
They answer only part of the question

questions.hint: Covering only part of the question loses marks.

questions.prompt: What is a helpful habit when practising with sample questions?

options.text: Memorising the exact wording of each of the questions
Writing a single answer that you can adapt to every question
Timing yourself on the Situation part only
Underlining the key phrases and checking your story covers them

questions.hint: Underlining key phrases keeps your answer on target.

questions.prompt: What is the hidden extra request in 'Describe a time you had to work with someone you found difficult'?

options.text: How you avoided working with them
How you stayed professional
Who was to blame for the problems
Why the person was difficult

questions.hint: The question tests your professional conduct.

questions.prompt: A question asks about delivering quickly without losing quality. Which two behaviours does it combine?

options.text: Working Together and Changing and Improving
Communicating and Influencing and Developing Self and Others
Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service
Leadership and Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: Speed and quality map to those two behaviours.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether an example from outside work is acceptable. What is a sensible approach?

options.text: Use a work example you do not remember well
Ask the panel whether it can come from anywhere
Skip the question and offer to return to it later
Answer a different question from the one asked

questions.hint: Asking for clarification is allowed.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I always work well in a team' a poor answer to a behaviour question?

options.text: It praises the candidate too highly
It is too short for the panel to hear properly
It is a general claim, not a specific moment
It uses the word 'I' instead of 'we'

questions.hint: Behaviour questions need a specific example.

questions.prompt: A question asks you to describe changing your plans. Which quality is it also testing?

options.text: How much you dislike having to change
How you coped with change and kept things on track
How often you have changed jobs
How well you can predict problems before they arise

questions.hint: It tests adaptability and control.

questions.prompt: Why do panels welcome sensible clarification questions?

options.text: They give the panel extra time to score
They show you want to answer accurately
They are scored as a separate item
They avoid the need for follow-up questions later

questions.hint: Careful candidates check what is meant.

items.title: Level 4: Comparing two answers and choosing the stronger
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: A useful way to learn is to compare answers. Imagine the question is 'Tell us about a time you helped a colleague.' Candidate A says: 'At work, we are very supportive. I often help people and they always say I am a team player. It is something I enjoy.' Candidate B says: 'Last month my colleague Priya was off sick and her customer emails were piling up. I asked my supervisor if I could take the oldest fifteen, checked her notes so I would answer correctly, and replied to all of them by the end of the next day. When she came back she said it saved her a week's worth of catching up, and she showed me how she sorted her inbox.' Candidate B's answer is much stronger. It is a specific event, with a name, a time, an action and a result. It shows the candidate asked permission, checked information and learned something. Candidate A's answer is a general claim with no evidence. A panel can only score what it can see. When you compare answers, look for four things. Is it one real event? Does it show what the candidate personally did? Is there a clear result? Does it match the question? Another point is balance. An answer that is full of detail about the situation but only says 'I sorted it out' about the action is weaker than one with the reverse. Finally, tone matters. Modesty is fine, but being so modest that you hide your own part makes it hard to score you well.

questions.prompt: Why is Candidate B's answer, about covering emails, stronger than Candidate A's general claim?

options.text: It includes praise from the supervisor
It mentions a colleague by name and so seems warmer
It is longer and uses more descriptive words
It describes a specific event with an action and a result

questions.hint: B gives evidence; A makes a general claim.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of Candidate A's answer?

options.text: It is a general claim with no evidence
It uses 'we' far too often
It describes a time that was too long ago
It is too specific to be of use

questions.hint: A panel can score only what it can see.

questions.prompt: Which detail in Candidate B's answer shows careful working?

options.text: Taking the oldest fifteen emails to answer first
Naming the colleague at the start of the story
Checking her notes so the replies would be correct
Describing why the colleague was away

questions.hint: Checking notes shows care for accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which detail in Candidate B's answer shows initiative within sensible limits?

options.text: Replying by the end of the next day
Asking the supervisor before taking the emails
Counting the number of emails to be answered
Mentioning the colleague who was away

questions.hint: Asking permission shows awareness of limits.

questions.prompt: What does the colleague's reaction add to Candidate B's answer?

options.text: A fuller description of the situation
A clear result
A further action
A weakness to discuss

questions.hint: The reaction shows the effect of the help.

questions.prompt: Which question is least useful when comparing two answers?

options.text: Which candidate sounds the more confident?
Does it show what the candidate did?
Is it one real event?
Is there a clear result?

questions.hint: Confidence alone does not show evidence.

questions.prompt: An answer gives a long description of the situation but says only 'I sorted it out' about the action. How does it compare with a balanced answer?

options.text: It is weaker because the action is thin
It is stronger because the context is clear
It is equal because both describe the same event
It is stronger because it is more modest

questions.hint: Action detail is what is scored.

questions.prompt: Why can being too modest cause problems?

options.text: It lowers the number of examples you can use
It hides your own part and makes you hard to score
It shortens the answer so much that it breaks the time limit
It makes the panel doubt that you can work in a team

questions.hint: The panel needs to see what you did.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'We always support each other and I do my bit.' What does the panel need before it can score this?

options.text: A longer description of the office culture
A list of colleagues the candidate has helped
A promise to keep helping in the new job
A specific moment showing what the candidate did

questions.hint: Panels need specific evidence.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an answer to 'match the question'?

options.text: It is about the same length as other answers
It gives evidence for the behaviour that was asked about
It comes from the same kind of job that the panel does
It repeats the same words that the question used

questions.hint: The example must fit what was asked.

items.title: Level 4: Applying with little experience or a gap in your history
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Many people applying for Administrative Officer jobs are changing career, returning after time away or have little formal work history. The Civil Service accepts applications from people with many different backgrounds, and AO roles do not normally require formal qualifications. In the interview, the panel wants evidence of behaviours, wherever it comes from. If you have been caring for a family member, you have probably organised appointments, kept records, dealt with professionals and coped under pressure. If you have been studying, you have met deadlines and worked in groups. If you have volunteered, you have probably served the public or supported a team. Think about what you actually did in each setting and describe it in work-related language: for example, 'I kept a diary of medical appointments for my father and made sure we had the right paperwork at each one.' That shows organisation and accuracy. If the panel asks about a gap in your work history, answer briefly and honestly without apologising. You could say, 'I took time out to care for a family member, and during that time I...' and then move to what you learned or what you did. Do not feel you have to give private details. After that, bring the conversation back to the job. Avoid saying 'I don't have much experience.' Instead, say what you have done and what you are ready to learn. Panels know that entry-level staff will receive training. They are looking for willingness and the right behaviours, not a perfect CV.

questions.prompt: What does a panel mainly want to see from candidates with little formal work history?

options.text: Proof that they have worked in government before
Evidence of the behaviours, wherever it comes from
A full list of the jobs held in the past five years
A reference from a former employer for every example

questions.hint: Behaviours can be shown in any setting.

questions.prompt: Which skills might caring for a family member help to show?

options.text: Management of a large team of paid staff
Experience of recruiting staff for a business
Technical knowledge of Civil Service computer systems
Organisation and accuracy with records and appointments

questions.hint: Caring often involves organisation and record keeping.

questions.prompt: Which phrasing best turns home experience into work language?

options.text: 'I did what I could, with a lot of help from others.'
'It was a difficult time for the whole family and we coped.'
'I helped out a bit with things at home when I could.'
'I kept a diary of appointments and checked we had the paperwork.'

questions.hint: Specific, work-related language shows skill.

questions.prompt: How should you answer a question about a gap in your work history?

options.text: In great detail, covering every reason for it
By saying that it is private and declining to answer
Briefly and honestly, without apologising
By moving the conversation on very quickly

questions.hint: A short honest answer works best.

questions.prompt: After you have explained a gap, what is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat the explanation in different words
Ask the panel whether the gap will affect your score
Wait for another question on the subject
Move on to what you learned or did and return to the job

questions.hint: Bring the conversation back to the job.

questions.prompt: Which statement is better than 'I don't have much experience'?

options.text: 'I know I am probably not the strongest candidate here.'
'I hope you will be willing to give me a chance.'
'Everyone has to start somewhere, after all.'
'I have done X and Y, and I am ready to learn the rest.'

questions.hint: State what you have done and your willingness to learn.

questions.prompt: Why do panels not expect a perfect CV for AO roles?

options.text: Panels do not read CVs before interviews
Entry-level staff will receive training
Most successful candidates are already in government
The job does not need any particular skills

questions.hint: Training is provided, so potential matters.

questions.prompt: What qualifications do AO roles normally ask for?

options.text: A recognised qualification in English and maths
A degree in a subject related to administration
At least two A levels at grade C or above
Usually none, as they are entry-level roles

questions.hint: AO roles are usually open to people without qualifications.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a sensible way to use experience of volunteering in a charity shop?

options.text: Explain that the work was unpaid so it may not count
Say it was only a short, informal job
Describe serving customers and handling cash
Leave it out and use only paid work for your examples

questions.hint: Volunteering provides real examples.

questions.prompt: How much private detail do you have to give about a period of caring or illness?

options.text: A written statement from a relative
Medical evidence from your doctor
Only what you are comfortable sharing
Everything that the panel asks about

questions.hint: You do not have to share private details.

items.title: Level 4: Handling follow-up and probing questions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: After you give an answer, the panel may ask follow-up questions, called probes. They are a normal and important part of the interview. The panel uses probes to find out more about what you personally did and to check that your story is real. Common probes include 'What did you say to them?', 'Why did you choose that approach?', 'What else did you consider?', 'How did you know it had worked?' and 'What would you do differently?' A probe is not a sign that you did badly. In fact, if the panel asks one, it often means they found your answer interesting enough to explore. To handle probes well, know your stories in detail. Remember who was involved, what the timeline was, what you said and why. Answer the probe directly, in a sentence or two, and then stop. Do not repeat the whole story. If you do not remember a detail, be honest and say what you do remember. Avoid changing facts between your first answer and your follow-up answer, as this makes the panel suspicious. If a probe asks what you would do differently, give a real answer. Saying 'nothing' sounds closed to learning. A good reply names one thing, such as starting earlier or asking for help sooner, and says why. Finally, use probes as a chance to show your thinking. For instance, if the panel asks why you chose a particular approach, you can mention the options you considered and the reason you rejected them.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason panels ask probing questions?

options.text: To fill the time allowed for each candidate
To find out more about what you personally did
To make the interview feel more demanding
To give weaker candidates a second chance

questions.hint: Probes dig into your own actions.

questions.prompt: What does it often mean if the panel asks a probe?

options.text: They have run out of other questions to ask
They found your answer worth exploring
They want you to start the answer again
They did not believe any part of your answer

questions.hint: A probe is not a sign of failure.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of a probe?

options.text: 'Why did you choose that approach?'
'Why do you want this job?'
'Tell us about a time you led a team.'
'What do you see as your strengths?'

questions.hint: Probes follow up on an answer already given.

questions.prompt: How should you answer a probe?

options.text: Directly, in a sentence or two, and then stop
By asking the panel to move on to something else
By giving a long and detailed account of the background
By repeating the whole story from the start

questions.hint: Keep it brief and relevant.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to change facts between your first answer and a follow-up?

options.text: It may raise your score by showing flexibility
It shows you have more examples ready
It makes the panel suspicious
It saves time in the interview

questions.hint: Consistency matters.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you cannot remember a detail?

options.text: Say so and share what you do remember
Say that you prefer not to answer
Give your best guess at the detail
Change to a different story

questions.hint: Honesty beats inventing a detail.

questions.prompt: What is the best kind of answer to 'What would you do differently?'

options.text: 'Nothing, I think it went as well as it could.'
'I would ask someone else to take over.'
One real change and the reason for it
A long list of everything that went wrong

questions.hint: A real reflection shows openness to learning.

questions.prompt: Why does the answer 'nothing' to 'What would you do differently?' sound weak?

options.text: It suggests the story was invented
It sounds closed to learning
It breaks the rules of the question
It is too short for the panel to score

questions.hint: Reflection shows growth.

questions.prompt: How can a probe about why you chose an approach help you?

options.text: You can show the options you considered and your reasoning
You can ask the panel to explain what they meant
You can correct the panel's notes
You can replace your original answer with a better one

questions.hint: Probes give you a chance to show your thinking.

questions.prompt: What helps you most with probes in advance?

options.text: Writing out the probes and avoiding them
Knowing your stories in detail
Preparing only one story in depth
Learning each story word for word

questions.hint: Detailed knowledge lets you respond naturally.

items.title: Level 4: Using time well inside an answer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Many people worry about how long to speak. A useful guide is that most people speak at around 130 to 160 words a minute, so a two-minute answer is roughly 260 to 320 words. In an interview you will not count words, but it helps to know that a two-minute answer is longer than you might think, and a half-minute answer is only a few sentences. A behaviour answer is usually most effective at around two minutes, though a panel will not stop you at exactly that length. Some departments tell you how long the interview will be and how many questions to expect. If you have a 40-minute interview with five or six behaviour questions, you will have no more than six to eight minutes per question, including the question itself and any follow-up. That means a two-minute main answer leaves time for a probe or two. You can plan this in advance. When you practise a story, record yourself and time the parts. A good split might be around fifteen seconds for the situation, ten for the task, ninety for the actions and fifteen to twenty for the result. If the panel signals they want to move on, for example by saying 'Thank you, that's helpful', stop at once. Do not carry on to squeeze in another point. Equally, if you are only thirty seconds into an answer and have nothing more to add, stop. Short and clear is better than padded.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many words is a two-minute spoken answer?

options.text: About 500 to 600 words
About 900 to 1000 words
About 60 to 90 words
About 260 to 320 words

questions.hint: At 130 to 160 words per minute, two minutes is around 260 to 320 words.

questions.prompt: Which answer length is usually most effective for a behaviour question?

options.text: Around thirty seconds
Around two minutes
Around six minutes
Around ten minutes

questions.hint: A two-minute answer is typical.

questions.prompt: In a 40-minute interview with five or six behaviour questions, roughly how long is available per question at most?

options.text: Ten to twelve minutes, including follow-up
Six to eight minutes, including follow-up
Two minutes exactly, including follow-up
Under one minute, including follow-up

questions.hint: Forty minutes divided by five or six is roughly six to eight minutes.

questions.prompt: Why does this timing leave room for a probe?

options.text: Probes replace the main answer
The panel adds extra minutes automatically
The main answer uses only part of the time
Probes are not counted in the interview time

questions.hint: A two-minute main answer leaves space for follow-up.

questions.prompt: In the suggested split, which part gets the most time?

options.text: The task
The result
The actions
The situation

questions.hint: Actions deserve the most time.

questions.prompt: If the panel says 'Thank you, that's helpful' and moves on, what should you do?

options.text: Stop at once
Repeat your result
Ask whether you can finish
Add one more point first

questions.hint: The panel is signalling that they have enough.

questions.prompt: If you are thirty seconds into an answer and have nothing more to add, what is best?

options.text: Add a story from a different job to fill the time
Stop, because short and clear beats padded
Repeat your main point until two minutes have passed
Ask the panel what else they would like to hear

questions.hint: Padding weakens an answer.

questions.prompt: How can you check the real length of your practice answers?

options.text: Ask a friend to guess how long it felt
Count the sentences on the page
Record yourself and time the parts
Read the answer silently once

questions.hint: Recording shows the actual timing.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long is a good Situation in the suggested split?

options.text: About two minutes
About five seconds
About one minute
About fifteen seconds

questions.hint: Keep the Situation brief.

questions.prompt: Why might a panel tell you in advance how long the interview will be?

options.text: So you can prepare your own questions
So you can check the scoring system
So you can arrange travel home
So you can plan your answers and pace

questions.hint: Knowing the time helps you pace answers.

items.title: Level 4: Solving common video interview problems
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Video interviews bring practical problems that are easy to prepare for. If your picture is dark or your face is in shadow, move so that the main light is in front of you, not behind. A lamp placed behind the screen and pointing at your face works well. If the picture freezes or lags, the cause is usually the internet connection. Close other programs, move closer to the router, and ask others in the house to pause streaming. If the problem continues, turn off your camera briefly and say so, or use the phone number in the invitation to explain. If you hear an echo, the cause is usually speakers and a microphone picking each other up, and wearing headphones solves it. If a child or pet enters the room, a calm apology and a quick resolution are fine. Panels understand home life. If someone knocks, apologise briefly and continue. Do not turn it into a long explanation. If your notes are allowed, keep them on one page and place them beside the camera so you can glance at them without turning away. Avoid reading from a script, because it is obvious on screen. If you want a screen to show something, only share it if asked. Close anything private first. Finally, check that your username on the call shows your real name, not a nickname or an email address, so the host knows who you are when you join.

questions.prompt: Your face appears dark on screen. What is the best fix?

options.text: Lower the camera angle so your face is lit from above
Put the main light in front of you
Move closer to the window behind you so it lights the room
Turn off all the lights in the room to cut the glare

questions.hint: Front lighting lights your face.

questions.prompt: The picture freezes repeatedly. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The time of day
The colour of your clothes
The panel's computer
The internet connection

questions.hint: Freezing is usually an internet issue.

questions.prompt: Which step might help a poor connection?

options.text: Turning up the volume on your speakers and microphone
Closing other programs and pausing streaming
Moving your camera to a higher position in the room
Using a larger screen so the picture is clearer

questions.hint: Reducing demand on the connection helps.

questions.prompt: If a poor connection continues, what is a sensible next step?

options.text: Tell the panel, and phone the number given if needed
Keep going without mentioning it
Switch to a new device without telling the panel
End the call and wait for them to contact you

questions.hint: Telling the panel and using the contact number is best.

questions.prompt: What usually causes an echo on a call?

options.text: Speakers and a microphone picking each other up
A slow internet speed on your side
The panel's camera settings
A dark room

questions.hint: Headphones prevent the feedback.

questions.prompt: What helps to stop an echo?

options.text: Using a smaller window
Speaking more quietly
Moving the camera further away
Wearing headphones

questions.hint: Headphones separate sound output from the microphone.

questions.prompt: A child enters the room during your answer. What is the best response?

options.text: Leave the call to deal with it
A calm, brief apology, then carry on
Pretend nothing has happened
Stop and explain the whole situation

questions.hint: Panels understand home life.

questions.prompt: Where is the best place to keep notes, if they are allowed?

options.text: Behind the screen
On the floor next to you
Under the keyboard
On one page beside the camera

questions.hint: Notes near the camera let you glance without turning away.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid reading from a script on video?

options.text: It is obvious on screen and sounds unnatural
The panel will mark down any use of notes
The camera cannot see paper properly
Reading aloud is against the rules

questions.hint: Scripts sound false.

questions.prompt: When should you share your screen?

options.text: Only if the panel asks you to
When you answer your first question
Whenever you want to show something
At the start, to show your notes

questions.hint: Only share when requested.

questions.prompt: Why check the name that shows on your call display?

options.text: So the panel can learn your nickname
So the host knows who you are when you join
So your email address is shown to them
So you can find the meeting link again

questions.hint: A real name helps the host admit you.

items.title: Level 4: Calming nerves with practical techniques
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Nerves are a normal reaction, and several techniques can help you to manage them. Preparation is the first. When you have practised your examples out loud several times, your mind has paths to follow even when adrenaline makes you less sharp. Practise with a friend, or talk to a mirror. Second, the night before, avoid cramming. Go through your notes once, then do something calming and sleep well. Third, on the day, take a short walk or do light stretching. Movement burns off excess adrenaline. Fourth, use slow breathing. Breathing in for four counts and out for six helps to lower your heart rate, because a longer out-breath signals the body to relax. Do this for a minute before you start. Fifth, change how you think about the nerves. Instead of telling yourself 'I'm terrified', say 'I'm excited and ready.' The physical feelings are almost the same, and the second view helps you to use the energy. Sixth, during the interview, speak slowly, pause between sentences and sip water. If you feel your heart racing, put both feet flat on the floor and notice the pressure. Finally, remember that the panel is not your enemy. Most panel members have been candidates themselves, and they want you to do well so that they can fill their vacancy. A mistake is not the end. You can pause, correct it and carry on.

questions.prompt: Why does practising examples aloud help with nerves?

options.text: It makes the panel ask easier questions
It removes the need for any notes at all
It gives your mind paths to follow when nervous
It guarantees that you will not forget any detail on the day

questions.hint: Practice gives you familiar paths.

questions.prompt: What is the best use of the night before the interview?

options.text: Watch videos about interview mistakes
Learn some entirely new examples
Go through your notes once, then rest well
Stay up late practising every answer again

questions.hint: Cramming can increase anxiety.

questions.prompt: How does light movement on the day help?

options.text: It changes the questions asked
It burns off excess adrenaline
It improves your memory of the advert
It makes you speak more quickly

questions.hint: Movement releases tension.

questions.prompt: Why is a longer out-breath helpful?

options.text: It slows down the clock on the call
It increases the amount of oxygen in your voice
It clears your mind of all thoughts
It signals the body to relax and lowers the heart rate

questions.hint: A longer exhale calms the body.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of saying 'I'm excited and ready' instead of 'I'm terrified'?

options.text: It makes the panel notice your confidence
It tells the panel to go easy on you
It removes the physical feelings entirely
It helps you use the energy rather than fear it

questions.hint: The feelings are similar, but the label helps.

questions.prompt: What can you do if you feel your heart racing during the interview?

options.text: Put both feet flat on the floor and notice it
Speak more quickly to get through the answer
Stand up and move around the room to calm down
Ask for a break and leave the call for a moment

questions.hint: Grounding helps you settle.

questions.prompt: How should you think about the panel?

options.text: As opponents in a competition with you
As judges looking for mistakes to catch
As strangers who do not care about the outcome
As people who want you to do well

questions.hint: Panels want strong candidates.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you make a mistake during the interview?

options.text: Pause, correct it and carry on
Ask the panel to ignore the answer
Apologise at length and start again
Say nothing and hope it was missed

questions.hint: A calm correction is enough.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a poor way to reduce nerves?

options.text: Having a light snack and a drink of water beforehand
Cramming new material on the morning of the interview
Practising your examples aloud the day before
Taking slow breaths for a minute before you begin

questions.hint: Last-minute cramming raises anxiety.

questions.prompt: Why practise with a friend or a mirror?

options.text: You become used to speaking your answers aloud
It stops you from ever forgetting your words
The mirror shows you what the panel will ask
The friend can help to write your answers for you

questions.hint: Speaking aloud builds familiarity.

items.title: Level 4: Common myths about interview advice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: There is a lot of advice about interviews, and some of it is wrong or out of date. Here are several myths and the truth. Myth: you must memorise perfect answers. In reality, memorised answers sound stiff, and they fall apart when a question is phrased differently. Prepare examples and notes instead. Myth: you should never admit you do not know something. In fact, honesty, with an explanation of how you would find out, is respected. Myth: a longer answer is always better. A clear two-minute answer beats a rambling five-minute one. Myth: the panel can see everything on your CV, so you need not mention it. Panels often have only your application and may not read every line, so you need to say what matters. Myth: if you do not get the job, you were not good enough. Often several candidates meet the standard and there are only a few vacancies, so you may pass and still not be offered a post. Myth: you should hide nerves completely. Admitting 'I'm a little nervous' once is fine and human, as long as you then carry on. Myth: you should fill every silence. A pause to think is normal and shows care. Myth: only the answers count, and the first and last minutes do not matter. In practice, a polite greeting and a courteous ending add to the general impression, though the scoring rests on evidence. Learning to separate fact from myth helps you prepare in a calmer, smarter way.

questions.prompt: Why are memorised answers a poor approach?

options.text: They sound stiff and break down if the question changes
They are banned by the Civil Service in interviews
They take longer to deliver than natural answers
They always run over the time the panel allows

questions.hint: Notes and flexible examples are better.

questions.prompt: What is a better approach than memorising perfect answers?

options.text: Copying answers from an online guide
Writing a detailed script of each answer
Relying on your memory of the advert
Preparing examples and short notes

questions.hint: Prepare notes, not scripts.

questions.prompt: What is the truth about saying you do not know something?

options.text: Honesty, with how you would find out, is respected
It suggests you cannot do the job at all
It always costs you marks, so it should be avoided
It is only acceptable on strengths questions

questions.hint: Honest answers are respected.

questions.prompt: Why is the idea that a longer answer is always better a myth?

options.text: A clear two-minute answer beats a rambling five-minute one
Panels mark answers by word count
Long answers use too much of the panel's time to score
Short answers are always scored higher

questions.hint: Clarity matters more than length.

questions.prompt: Why should you not assume the panel has read everything on your application?

options.text: Panels never see applications before the interview
They may not read every line, so say what matters
The application is destroyed after the sift
They ask to see a printed copy at the start

questions.hint: Say what matters.

questions.prompt: If you pass but are not offered a job, what might be the explanation?

options.text: The reserve list only takes later applicants to the job
The panel found the interview unsatisfactory overall
The candidate gave some wrong answers to key questions
Several candidates met the standard but there were few vacancies

questions.hint: Passing does not guarantee an offer.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible approach to nerves?

options.text: Hiding every sign of nerves from the panel
Admitting once that you are a little nervous, then carrying on
Asking the panel to go easy on you
Apologising throughout for being nervous

questions.hint: A brief admission is fine.

questions.prompt: Why is a pause to think a good thing?

options.text: It shows care and gives you thinking time
It shows you have no answer to give
It is not allowed in a scored interview
It makes the panel impatient with you

questions.hint: Pauses are normal.

questions.prompt: What is the truth about the first and last minutes of an interview?

options.text: A courteous greeting and ending help the impression
They are scored separately from the answers
They carry most of the marks in the whole interview
They are not seen by the panel at all

questions.hint: Scoring depends on evidence, but manners help.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of separating fact from myth?

options.text: You can avoid practising out loud
You can skip reading the advert
You can predict the exact questions
You can prepare in a calmer, smarter way

questions.hint: Knowing the truth reduces worry.

items.title: Level 4: Researching the department and the role
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Researching the department shows interest and helps you to answer 'Why do you want to work here?' You do not need to become an expert. Aim for a few solid, accurate points that you can talk about naturally. Start with the department's page on GOV.UK. This gives its purpose, the services it provides and recent news. Look at its 'About us' page, its priorities and its list of agencies and public bodies. If the job is in an agency, read the agency's page too, as it may be the organisation you actually work for. Next, read the job advert again to see what the team does, and search for the team's work on GOV.UK. If the role involves a public service, such as processing benefits or issuing documents, find the guidance for users and see what they are asked to do. Try to understand who uses the service. Note one or two facts or recent developments that interest you, and think about why. Also learn what the department values. Many publish their purpose and values, and these often echo the Civil Service Code. Prepare a short answer to 'What do you know about us?' that covers what the department does, who it serves and one thing that appeals to you. Keep it brief. Do not recite long lists of facts or quote figures you are unsure about. If you make a claim, be able to explain it. You can also mention how your experience links to the work.

questions.prompt: Where is a good place to start researching a department?

options.text: A general website about careers
A news article from several years ago
Its page on GOV.UK
A social media post by an employee

questions.hint: GOV.UK pages are authoritative.

questions.prompt: What can the department's 'About us' page tell you?

options.text: The questions you will be asked on the day
The scores needed to pass the interview stage
The names of the interview panel members who will see you
Its purpose, priorities and connected bodies

questions.hint: It outlines what the department does.

questions.prompt: Why might you read the agency's page as well as the department's?

options.text: Agencies pay the salary of the interview panel
Agency pages list all vacancies in the department
The agency may be the organisation you actually work for
Agencies set the interview questions

questions.hint: An agency can be the actual employer.

questions.prompt: If the role involves a public service, what extra research is useful?

options.text: The names of the ministers responsible
The salaries of the staff who deliver it
The guidance given to people who use the service
The history of the building where the team sits

questions.hint: User guidance shows the service's purpose.

questions.prompt: How many points should you aim to be able to talk about?

options.text: A few solid, accurate points
As many facts as you can remember
Every detail from the website
Only one fact, to avoid errors

questions.hint: A few accurate points are enough.

questions.prompt: What should a short answer to 'What do you know about us?' include?

options.text: What the department does, who it serves and one thing that appeals
A long list of facts and figures about the budget
A summary of recent political debates about the department
The names of senior officials and their career histories

questions.hint: Cover purpose, users and your interest.

questions.prompt: Why avoid quoting figures you are unsure about?

options.text: You must be able to explain any claim you make
Figures take too long to say in a short answer
Figures are not allowed in Civil Service interviews
Panels dislike numbers in answers as a rule

questions.hint: Only use facts you can explain.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to know the department's values?

options.text: They are used to score your answers
They often echo the Civil Service Code
They show the salary scale for the grade
They list the questions the panel will ask

questions.hint: Values link to the Code.

questions.prompt: How can you link your experience to the department's work?

options.text: Describe how you would improve it
Compare it favourably with another department
Say how something you did relates to its work
Say you have always wanted to work in government

questions.hint: Linking experience shows relevance.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of this research?

options.text: To impress the panel with difficult words
To recite as many facts as possible
To avoid being asked behaviour questions
To show interest and give a genuine reason

questions.hint: Research supports a genuine answer.

items.title: Level 4: How panels keep interviews fair
items.body: Fairness in Civil Service recruitment rests on several practical features. First, structured interviews. Every candidate for the same job is asked the same core questions, in a similar order, so answers can be compared on the same basis. Second, assessment against criteria. The panel scores answers against the behaviours or strengths in the advert and uses a scoring guide that explains what poor, acceptable and strong evidence looks like. This reduces the risk that someone is scored on liking or on shared background. Third, independent scoring. Each panel member usually scores separately before they compare notes, so one strong voice cannot dominate. Fourth, training. Panel members are trained in interviewing and in avoiding bias, which is the tendency to favour or disadvantage people for reasons unrelated to the job, such as accent or age. Fifth, note-taking. Written notes provide a record of the evidence behind each score. This also means candidates can ask for feedback, and the recruitment team can check that decisions were reasonable. Sixth, adjustments. Candidates with disabilities or other needs can ask for changes so that they can show their ability. Seventh, the Recruitment Principles, overseen by the Civil Service Commission, require appointments to be on merit following fair and open competition. If a candidate believes a recruitment process has breached the Principles, they can complain first to the department and then, if still dissatisfied, to the Civil Service Commission.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a structured interview?

options.text: To shorten the time each interview takes
To let the panel choose different questions for each person
To compare candidates' answers on the same basis
To avoid taking notes

questions.hint: Same questions allow fair comparison.

questions.prompt: What does a scoring guide help the panel to do?

options.text: Judge strong and weak evidence consistently
Change the criteria after each interview
Reduce the number of questions asked in total
Decide who to hire before the interviews begin

questions.hint: A scoring guide explains levels of evidence.

questions.prompt: Why do panel members usually score separately before comparing?

options.text: So that they do not need to take notes
So that candidates can see all of the scores
So that one strong voice cannot dominate
So that they can save time afterwards

questions.hint: Independent scoring reduces influence.

questions.prompt: What is bias in an interview?

options.text: A method of recording what candidates say
A rule that sets out how answers are scored
Favouring or disadvantaging people for reasons unrelated to the job
A type of question that tests several behaviours

questions.hint: Bias is unfair favouring based on irrelevant factors.

questions.prompt: How does training help the panel?

options.text: It helps them to interview well and avoid bias
It removes the need to follow the criteria
It tells them which candidates to prefer
It gives them the right to change the questions

questions.hint: Training reduces bias.

questions.prompt: Why do written notes make the process fairer?

options.text: They give a record of the evidence behind each score
They show how long each candidate spoke
They allow candidates to see other candidates' scores
They replace the need for criteria

questions.hint: Notes provide a basis for review and feedback.

questions.prompt: Who oversees the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: The chair of the panel
The Treasury
The Civil Service Commission
The candidate's local council

questions.hint: The Commission oversees the Principles.

questions.prompt: What do the Recruitment Principles require?

options.text: Appointments agreed by ministers
Appointments of people who already work in government
Appointments on merit after fair and open competition
Appointments made by lottery among qualified applicants

questions.hint: Merit and fair open competition are required.

questions.prompt: If you believe the Principles were breached, what is the usual first step?

options.text: Contact the Prime Minister
Ask the panel to reverse the decision
Post about it online
Complain to the department

questions.hint: You complain to the department first.

questions.prompt: Where can you take a complaint if you remain dissatisfied?

options.text: The Cabinet Office press office
The panel's line manager
A national newspaper
The Civil Service Commission

questions.hint: The Commission can look at complaints.

items.title: Level 4: Feedback, reserve lists and security checks
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles and GOV.UK guidance
items.body: After the decision, feedback is one of the most valuable things you can receive. Feedback usually tells you your overall result and, for each behaviour or strength, how you did. Read it carefully and look for patterns across the answers. If several comments say that your examples lacked detail on the action, that is the thing to fix. Do not take comments personally. They describe the answers on the day, not you as a person. If the feedback is unclear, you can ask the recruitment team a polite follow-up question. If you pass and are placed on a reserve list, you may be offered a post for as long as the list is valid, which is stated in your letter or on the advert. Keep your contact details up to date and respond promptly if you hear from the team, as unanswered contact might lead them to move to the next person. Placement on a list does not guarantee an offer. If you receive an offer, it will be conditional on checks. The Baseline Personnel Security Standard is the minimum, verifying identity, right to work, employment history and unspent criminal convictions. Some roles require higher levels of security clearance, such as Counter-Terrorist Check or Security Check, which involve further questions and take longer. Be honest and complete on forms. Mistakes or omissions can delay the process or lead to an offer being withdrawn. If you are unsure about something, ask the vetting team how to answer rather than leaving it out.

questions.prompt: What does feedback usually include?

options.text: Your overall result and how you did on each behaviour
The questions that will be used next time
The scores of all the other candidates
The names of the panel members who scored you

questions.hint: Feedback is specific to your answers.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to read feedback?

options.text: Ignore anything about your examples
Look for a reason to disagree with the panel
Look for patterns across the comments
Focus on the single harshest comment

questions.hint: Patterns show what to improve.

questions.prompt: Why should you not take feedback personally?

options.text: It is written by people who dislike you personally
It is only a formality that is rarely read closely
It describes the answers on the day, not you
It rarely contains any useful detail for candidates

questions.hint: Feedback is about your performance.

questions.prompt: How long might a reserve list stay valid?

options.text: For a period stated in your letter or the advert
For the rest of your working life in the Civil Service
For one week exactly after the results are sent
Until the next round of interviews takes place

questions.hint: The validity period is stated by the department.

questions.prompt: Why should you respond quickly if the team contacts you from a reserve list?

options.text: They will raise your score for replying
They will reduce the pay offered if you wait
They might move on to the next person
The list ends on the same day

questions.hint: Unanswered contact can lead them to move on.

questions.prompt: What does placement on a reserve list mean for a job offer?

options.text: It guarantees promotion after six months
It guarantees the first vacancy that arises
It guarantees a job in the same team
It may lead to an offer, but there is no guarantee

questions.hint: A reserve place may or may not lead to a job.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum security check for many roles?

options.text: Developed Vetting at the highest level
Security Check for sensitive posts
The Baseline Personnel Security Standard
Counter-Terrorist Check for sensitive posts

questions.hint: BPSS is the baseline.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the Baseline Personnel Security Standard verify?

options.text: Your medical records and health history in full
Identity, right to work, work history and unspent convictions
Your political views and the groups you belong to
Your credit rating and bank balance over many years

questions.hint: These are the elements of BPSS.

questions.prompt: How do higher security clearances differ from BPSS?

options.text: They are quicker and simpler to complete
They are only checked after the job begins
They apply to everyone at the same level
They involve further questions and take longer

questions.hint: Higher levels need more checks.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you are unsure how to answer a question on a vetting form?

options.text: Leave it blank and mention it later
Make your best guess and move on
Ask a friend to answer it for you
Ask the vetting team how to answer

questions.hint: Ask rather than omit.
